summary:
Guanajuato operates within Mexico's framework for legal gender recognition, which is set state by state rather than by a single national statute. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of the country's 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, that two more run one in practice without enactment, that six state legislatures have enacted nothing, and that only seven states extend recognition to children. The Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation set binding guidelines for the states in 2022 and extended the right to minors that year, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. None of the sources for this record states which of those four categories Guanajuato occupies.

What the sources do place in Guanajuato is documented harm. Human Rights Watch records incidents in the state where identity documents that do not match a trans person's gender drive discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, which is the consequence the same report describes wherever no recognition procedure exists.

The clearest evidence of what a silent state statute means on the ground comes from Tabasco, a Mexican state with no legal gender-recognition procedure. The Human Rights Watch and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024 found that without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance-based scrutiny carries a risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and that trans people are shut out of employment, health services, education and financial transactions. That report was written in the aftermath of the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gómez in Villahermosa, in a country where more than 95% of homicides went unpunished in 2022.

Lethal violence against trans people carries a dedicated offence in only two of Mexico's 32 states, and Guanajuato is not one of them. Mexico City's Congress passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide with penalties of up to 70 years, after Nayarit became the first state to do so with a maximum of 60 years. Impunity for transfemicide is thought to run higher than the national homicide figure.
tangentialFactors:
Formal rights and their enforcement diverge across Mexico. Analysis published by Caroline Beer on the LSE USAPP blog on 22 November 2024 found that the country's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist on paper but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and Beer stated explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Trans killings continue to draw protest and monitoring. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which triggered street demonstrations. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and the murder of LGBTI+ defenders had increased over the previous year. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a total second only to Brazil's 100.

The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.
localsOnly:
Guanajuato's authorities stand under binding guidelines set by the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation in 2022, which also extended legal gender recognition to minors that year, and under the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requirement of a simple, accessible procedure. Whether the state's own administrative bodies apply those guidelines in practice is not addressed by these sources.

Residents whose identity documents do not match their gender face exclusion from employment, health services, education and financial transactions, and every document request or appearance-based scrutiny carries a risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, according to the findings documented in Tabasco and cited by Human Rights Watch for Guanajuato.

Guanajuato has not enacted a transfemicide statute; only Mexico City, with a maximum of 70 years, and Nayarit, with a maximum of 60 years, have done so. Lethal violence against trans residents is therefore prosecuted under ordinary homicide provisions, in a national context where more than 95% of homicides went unpunished in 2022 and impunity for transfemicide is thought to be higher still.
